text: in/qa-history-tools fe4c76a6 is approved by the owner's brain and LANDED as 53d4eddd (owner asked for it; tests 27/27 in the copy, no entry point was run). The review found no way to aim the tool at the real system: the allow-list in assertQaUrl, the pg client guard, the socket fence and the server-side current_database()/role checks hold. These are required in the NEXT branch that touches tools/qa-six-month (the startup one), before it can land: [MEDIUM] runtime.mjs startRuntime (about 54-100) with run.mjs optionsOf (repo defaults to process.cwd()): when qa.env is absent the tool reads <repo>/apps/api/.env and does mkdir of the run directory before assertQaUrl runs, and --repo silently defaults to the current directory. Run from the wrong checkout it loads that checkout's secrets into memory and leaves a directory there before refusing on the port. Wanted: --repo is mandatory with --apply (no cwd default); the target check runs before any mkdir or .env read; credentials do not come from apps/api/.env: require a pre-provisioned qa.env or an explicit BTO_QA_DATABASE_URL that passes assertQaUrl. [LOW] safety.test.mjs: add table-driven refusals: a URL on another port with the QA database name, localhost, [::1], 127.0.0.2, a LAN address, ?host=/?port= overrides, assertClientTarget, startRuntime without explicitlyEnabled / database / password, assertRunDirectory escaping the run directory. [LOW] ADR-0247: one paragraph that the tool must never run against the real system and how that is enforced (hard-coded 127.0.0.1:15432/<QA db>, current_database() and role checks, refusal of a non-empty database without its own checkpoint); it is written for a Windows PC only: say what holds on the Ubuntu PC that hosts the real system. [LOW] README, ADR-0247, journal.mjs: the repository is public: use neutral wording instead of a person's local database name and login (a generic QA admin name) and no internal paths beyond the tool's own run directory. [LOW] dataset.mjs 431-440: drop the «Оргил» prefix from the fictional customer names; it reads like the company's own name.
